lesson.title: What People Actually Need: Autonomy, Competence, and Connection
lesson.summary: Self-determination theory, developed by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, proposes that human motivation and well being flourish when three innate psychological needs, autonomy, competence, and relatedness, are satisfied.
lesson.body:
Drive-reduction theory explains motivation mainly through biological deficits: hunger, thirst, and similar internal imbalances create uncomfortable states that push an organism to act until balance is restored. That framework works well for biological needs, but it struggles to explain why people pursue activities, like a challenging hobby or a demanding creative project, that offer no obvious biological payoff and sometimes even involve real discomfort along the way. Self-determination theory addresses a different category of need entirely: not deficits that must be corrected, but psychological needs whose satisfaction actively promotes growth, engagement, and well being rather than simply relieving discomfort.

The theory also shares common ground with social-cognitive theory in treating people as active agents rather than passive responders to reward and punishment. Deci and Ryan place particular weight on autonomy, the sense that one's actions are chosen and self-endorsed rather than imposed by external control, which closely parallels the sense of personal agency that runs through Bandura's account of self-efficacy and reciprocal influence between person, behavior, and environment.

Self-determination theory identifies three needs it argues are innate and important across cultures and contexts. Autonomy is the sense of volition, of acting from one's own values and interests rather than feeling controlled or coerced. Competence is the sense of being effective, of being able to meet challenges and see the results of one's efforts. Relatedness is the sense of being connected to, understood by, and cared for by other people. When an environment, a classroom, a workplace, a family, tends to support these three needs, people typically show more sustained, higher quality motivation and greater well being. When an environment consistently thwarts them, through excessive external control, unclear or discouraging feedback, or social isolation, motivation and well being both tend to suffer.

One of the theory's most influential contributions is the idea that motivation is not simply present or absent, it varies in kind, ranging from fully controlled, doing something only because of external pressure, to fully autonomous, doing something because it aligns with one's own values or is inherently enjoyable. That range sets up the classic distinction covered next, between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation.
